name: Nefazodone (Serzone)
summary: Prescription antidepressant for major depression that can be calming and sleep-friendly for some people, but it carries a rare, serious liver failure risk. Requires strict symptom awareness and liver-safety screening.
description: Nefazodone is an antidepressant used for depression. Some people feel less anxious, less “on edge,” and sleep a bit better once it starts working, but it is NOT a casual med because of its boxed warning for rare, life-threatening liver injury. You should not start it if you have active liver disease or elevated baseline liver enzymes. If you develop signs of liver trouble (yellow eyes/skin, nausea, loss of appetite, stomach pain, dark urine, unusual fatigue), stop the medication and contact your prescriber immediately.
patient_summary: Nefazodone treats depression and can feel calming for some people, but it has a rare, serious liver failure risk. Don’t start it with active liver disease or high liver enzymes. Learn the liver warning signs (jaundice, nausea, loss of appetite, GI complaints, malaise) and report them immediately.

linked_conditions.context: Used to treat major depression. Early benefits may show up in 1 to 2 weeks, with continued improvement through 4 to 6 weeks.
Not a primary sleep medication, but some people notice calmer nights and easier sleep as depression and hyperarousal improve. Sedation can occur, so timing and dose strategy matter.
Some patients with depression plus anxiety feel less keyed-up on nefazodone, but it’s not a first-line anxiety medication and liver risk heavily limits its role.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to nefazodone, related compounds (phenylpiperazines), or any component of the formulation
Liver injury due to previous nefazodone treatment
Concurrent therapy with triazolam is generally contraindicated (if used, triazolam dose reduction may be required but may not be feasible with available dosage forms)

efficacy_response.patient_text: With depression medications like nefazodone, you usually don’t feel a “flip switch” on day one. Some people notice early changes (less emotional intensity, better sleep, less agitation) within 1 to 2 weeks, with fuller antidepressant benefits building over 4 to 6 weeks.
efficacy_response.citation_tag: Product labeling; clinical references cited in notes

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Rapid; well absorbed (food delays absorption and may reduce bioavailability)
pharmacokinetics.onset: Depression: early effects may appear within 1-2 weeks; continued improvement through 4-6 weeks
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: About 1 hour (prolonged when taken with food)
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Parent drug: 2-4 hours; active metabolites persist longer
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic (n-dealkylation and hydroxylation) to multiple metabolites including hydroxynefazodone (active) and m-chlorophenylpiperazine (active)
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Food delays absorption (~20%) and can reduce bioavailability (~20%); taking after meals may reduce lightheadedness but can also reduce effectiveness for some patients

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Nefazodone is used to treat depression. In real-world psychiatry, it’s sometimes considered when other antidepressants haven’t worked or weren’t tolerated—especially if insomnia, agitation, or sexual side effects have been a problem on SSRIs. The tradeoff is big: nefazodone has a boxed warning for rare, life-threatening liver failure, so it’s a “serious conversation” medication, not a casual first pick.
items: {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)}: Persistent low mood, loss of interest, impaired sleep, appetite changes, low energy, and impaired functioning
off_label: Depression with prominent insomnia (as mood settles, sleep may improve)
Depression with agitation or anxiety symptoms (some patients feel less keyed-up)
Patients who had unacceptable sexual side effects on SSRIs (nefazodone is often lower-risk here, but not zero-risk)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Everyone’s experience is different, but these are common patterns people describe when nefazodone works (and when it doesn’t):

quotes: It wasn’t like caffeine or a benzo. It was more like… the fog started thinning over a couple weeks.
I didn’t feel “happy,” but I felt less raw and less reactive.
Week two was the first time I noticed I wasn’t spiraling as hard.
My body felt less wired at night, so sleep came easier.
It took the edge off my agitation, but it also made me a little sleepy.
I could finally stop doom-scrolling at 2 a.m. because my brain felt quieter.
items.note: Sedation can happen, especially early on or with dose increases. Timing doses and going up slowly matters.

items.category: Side effect vibe: dry mouth + dizziness
quotes: Dry mouth was annoying at first—like I needed water constantly.
I got lightheaded standing up too fast.
A little dizziness in the beginning, then it mostly faded.
items.note: Lightheadedness can be worse if you jump up quickly. Taking doses after meals may reduce postural symptoms for some people.

items.category: Mood activation warning signs (call your prescriber)
quotes: I felt weirdly restless and agitated after a dose increase.
My sleep dropped but my energy went up in a not-good way.
I started acting impulsive and it didn’t feel like ‘me.’
items.note: Any sudden agitation, insomnia, panic-y energy, irritability, hostility, impulsivity, akathisia, hypomania, or mania—especially early in treatment or during dose changes—needs quick medical attention.

items.category: The liver warning is real (don’t ignore symptoms)
quotes: I was fine… until I wasn’t. When I got unusually tired and nauseated, my doctor told me to stop and get labs.
The liver warning made me pay attention to symptoms I’d normally brush off.
If you notice yellow eyes or weird stomach symptoms, don’t ‘wait it out.’
items.note: The rare liver risk is the reason this medication isn’t commonly used as a first-line option.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Nefazodone isn’t an “immediate relief” medication. It’s an antidepressant, so the benefits build over time—especially for mood and emotional heaviness.
key_points: 1-2 weeks: Some people notice early changes (less agitation, slightly better sleep, less emotional intensity)
4-6 weeks: Fuller antidepressant benefit is more likely to show up
About 1 hour: Peak blood level after a dose in adults (can be delayed by food)
2-4 hours: Parent drug half-life (active metabolites can hang around longer)
Food effect: Food can delay absorption and reduce bioavailability; dosing after meals may reduce lightheadedness for some, but can also reduce effectiveness

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Most people won’t feel a dramatic change immediately. When nefazodone helps, early signs often appear within the first couple weeks, with more meaningful improvement building over 4 to 6 weeks. If nothing is moving by that point—mood, sleep, energy, thinking—your prescriber will usually reassess dose, diagnosis (including bipolar screening), and whether it’s worth continuing given the liver risk.
sections.clinical_details: Clinical references describe early effects within 1 to 2 weeks and continued improvements through 4 to 6 weeks for depression. Because this medication carries a serious liver warning, the risk–benefit bar is higher than for many other antidepressants, and continuation should be tied to clear clinical benefit.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Boxed warnings: suicidality risk (especially ages ≤24) and rare, life-threatening liver failure.
sections.black_box: Antidepressants increase the risk of suicidal thinking and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults in short-term studies. Patients of all ages starting antidepressants should be monitored closely for clinical worsening, suicidality, and unusual behavior changes—especially in the first 1 to 2 months and during dose changes. Nefazodone is not approved for pediatric use. Separately, cases of life-threatening hepatic failure have occurred with nefazodone; treatment should not ordinarily be started in people with active liver disease or elevated baseline transaminases, and the medication must be stopped immediately if symptoms suggest liver injury or if AST/ALT rise to ≥3 times the upper limit of normal.
other: Liver failure warning: Rare but severe, including cases requiring transplant or causing death; reported U.S. rate about 1 case of liver failure resulting in death or transplant per 250,000 to 300,000 patient-years

Stop immediately and call your clinician if you develop signs of liver dysfunction: jaundice, loss of appetite, nausea/GI complaints, malaise, unusual fatigue, dark urine, or right-upper-abdominal discomfort
Do not re-challenge: If you develop hepatocellular injury (AST/ALT ≥3x ULN) on nefazodone, you should be withdrawn and generally should not be restarted
Suicidality risk pattern: Increased risk vs placebo in ages 24 and younger; no increase beyond age 24 in short-term studies; decreased risk in adults ≥65 in short-term studies
Mania/hypomania risk: Any antidepressant can unmask bipolar disorder; screen for bipolar disorder before treating depressive symptoms
CNS depression: Can impair alertness; be careful with driving/operating machinery until you know how you respond
Orthostatic hypotension: Can cause lightheadedness when standing; higher risk with dehydration, cardiovascular disease, or interacting meds
Narrow-angle glaucoma risk: Mild pupillary dilation can trigger an attack in susceptible individuals
patient_counseling: If you’re under 25, your prescriber should watch you more closely early on and after dose changes. Families/caregivers should know what to look for: worsening depression, suicidal thoughts, agitation, panic attacks, insomnia, irritability, hostility, impulsivity, akathisia, hypomania/mania.
Know the liver red flags and treat them like an emergency-level warning: yellow eyes/skin, loss of appetite, nausea, stomach complaints, malaise, unusual fatigue, dark urine. Don’t wait.
Do not start if you have active liver disease or elevated baseline liver enzymes unless your prescriber has a very specific reason and a monitoring plan.
Don’t mix with interacting medications without a prescriber’s sign-off—nefazodone has major interaction potential (especially via CYP3A4).
Ask for the smallest practical prescription quantity when risk is higher, and keep close follow-up early in treatment.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common side effects include headache, dry mouth, nausea, drowsiness, dizziness, constipation, insomnia, and agitation. Some people also experience lightheadedness from orthostatic hypotension. Rare but serious risks include liver injury/failure and severe mood changes.
plain_language_list: Dizziness or lightheadedness (especially standing up quickly)
Insomnia or agitation (especially early or with dose changes)
Blurred vision or other visual changes

common.patient_note: Headache is one of the most common complaints. Hydration, sleep regularity, and timing doses consistently can help; persistent or severe headaches should be discussed with your prescriber.
Dry mouth can be surprisingly intense at first. Water, sugar-free gum/lozenges, and good dental hygiene matter because chronic dry mouth can affect teeth and gums.
Nausea is common early on. Some people do better taking it with food, but food can also reduce absorption—so if your symptoms are controlled, your prescriber may help you find the best routine.
Sedation can be helpful if insomnia is part of the depression, but it can also feel like a daytime drag. Don’t drive or do risky tasks until you know how you react.
This can include a ‘stand up and see stars’ feeling. Hydration, slower position changes, and taking after meals may reduce postural symptoms for some people.
Yes—some people feel calmer, others feel more wired. If sleep worsens or agitation ramps up, especially after a dose change, call your prescriber.
Fiber, fluids, and routine movement help. If constipation becomes severe or painful, talk with your clinician.
Agitation early in treatment can overlap with the suicidality warning symptoms (restlessness, irritability, panic-y energy). Treat it seriously and report it quickly.

serious: Liver injury/failure: jaundice, anorexia, nausea/GI complaints, malaise, dark urine, unusual fatigue; stop medication and seek urgent evaluation
Hepatocellular injury labs: AST/ALT ≥3 times ULN while on nefazodone requires stopping and avoiding re-challenge
Severe mood activation: hypomania/mania, extreme agitation, impulsivity, hostility; urgent clinical reassessment
Suicidal ideation or abrupt behavioral change (especially early treatment or during dose changes): urgent evaluation
Orthostatic hypotension with falls or fainting
Priapism (rare but serious): prolonged painful erection requires emergency care
Serotonin syndrome (rare, usually with interacting serotonergic meds): agitation, confusion, fever, tremor, sweating, diarrhea; medical emergency

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Nefazodone has major interaction potential. It strongly inhibits CYP3A4 and can raise levels of certain medications to dangerous ranges. This is one of the biggest practical barriers to using it safely.

items.risk: Contraindicated combination per labeling. Interaction risk and loss of safe predictability.
items.action: Avoid. Choose a different antidepressant or different anticonvulsant strategy with specialist guidance.

items.risk: Generally contraindicated; if used, triazolam dose reduction may be required (very large reductions may be needed and may not be feasible with available dosage forms).
items.action: Avoid if possible. If there is no alternative, this needs specialist-level planning and careful monitoring.

items.risk: High risk when overlapping antidepressants with MAOI activity due to dangerous reactions.
items.action: Wait 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting nefazodone; wait at least 7 days between stopping nefazodone and starting an MAOI.

items.with: Other sedating medications (sleep aids, antihistamines, alcohol, opioids)
items.risk: Additive CNS depression: more sedation, impaired coordination, and higher accident risk.
items.action: Use extreme caution. Avoid alcohol. Discuss all sedating meds with your prescriber before combining.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: When stopping an antidepressant after it’s been used for more than a few weeks, tapering helps reduce withdrawal-type symptoms and helps you (and your clinician) spot relapse early. With nefazodone, evidence for the perfect taper schedule is limited, but a gradual reduction is commonly used—especially at higher doses or if you’ve had discontinuation symptoms before.
key_points: If treatment lasted ≥4 weeks: a gradual taper over ~2 weeks is commonly used to reduce withdrawal symptoms and monitor for returning depression symptoms
If treatment was brief (2-3 weeks): taper over 1-2 weeks may be reasonable; if <2 weeks, a taper is often not necessary
Go slower (e.g., ~4 weeks or longer) if you’ve had prior discontinuation symptoms, you’re on higher doses, or you’re very sensitive to dose changes
If withdrawal symptoms become intolerable: resume the previous dose and taper more gradually
Some clinicians discontinue nefazodone without tapering regardless of duration, but data supporting that approach are limited; a cautious taper is often the safer default

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Nefazodone is usually dosed twice daily. Doses are increased slowly based on response and tolerability, typically no more often than weekly. Because of serious interaction potential and the boxed liver warning, dosing should be individualized and conservative.

adult.depression_initial: 100 mg PO twice daily; some guidelines suggest starting lower (50 to 100 mg/day total) depending on tolerability
adult.depression_titration: Increase gradually by 100 to 200 mg/day (in 2 divided doses) at intervals of at least 1 week based on response and side effects
adult.depression_typical: 150 to 600 mg/day total in 2 divided doses
adult.older_adult_initial: 50 mg PO twice daily; increase gradually based on response and tolerability
adult.renal: No manufacturer-provided adjustment; adjustment unlikely because renal impairment does not appear to alter steady-state nefazodone plasma concentrations
adult.hepatic: Use with caution; exposure (AUC) is ~25% higher in cirrhosis. Do not ordinarily initiate in active liver disease or elevated baseline transaminases. Contraindicated in patients with liver injury due to previous nefazodone treatment.

sections.simple_explanation: Most people take nefazodone twice a day. The dose is increased slowly (usually weekly) to balance antidepressant benefit with side effects like sedation, dizziness, and lightheadedness. Liver safety and drug interactions are central to safe prescribing with this medication.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Nefazodone is not a first-line antidepressant in pregnancy or breastfeeding, mainly because there are limited outcome data and because safer, better-studied options exist. If someone is already stable on an effective antidepressant, decisions during pregnancy are usually made through shared decision-making that weighs relapse risk against medication risk.
sections.pregnancy: Pregnancy outcome data with nefazodone are limited. Untreated or undertreated depression during pregnancy carries real risks (relapse, impaired functioning, and adverse pregnancy outcomes). If medication is needed, clinicians often prefer better-studied antidepressants first. If a patient is already doing well on an effective regimen, continuation may be considered unless a contraindication exists. Use the lowest effective dose of a single agent when possible, and monitor symptoms regularly with a validated scale during pregnancy as part of shared decision-making.
sections.lactation: Nefazodone and active metabolites can be present in breast milk, and case reports describe possible infant effects (drowsiness, lethargy, poor feeding), especially in vulnerable infants (e.g., premature). If breastfeeding while taking nefazodone is considered, weigh infant age and health, maternal benefit, and alternative options. Monitor the infant for sedation and feeding issues, and involve pediatrics when needed.
sections.pediatrics: Not approved for pediatric patients. Antidepressants as a class carry increased suicidality risk in children, adolescents, and young adults, and nefazodone specifically is not approved in children.
sections.geriatrics: Older adults may have higher exposure (higher Cmax/AUC). Start lower (e.g., 50 mg twice daily) and increase slowly. Watch closely for sedation, dizziness, and orthostatic hypotension to reduce fall risk.
sections.hepatic: Use with caution; increased exposure in cirrhosis. Do not ordinarily initiate in active liver disease or elevated baseline transaminases. If AST/ALT rise to ≥3x ULN or symptoms suggest liver injury, stop immediately and do not reintroduce.
sections.renal: Use with caution in renal impairment. No manufacturer-provided adjustment; changes are generally unlikely based on available steady-state data.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Liver safety: Baseline liver function tests (AST/ALT). Periodic monitoring may be used, but symptom-based vigilance is critical. If AST/ALT rise to ≥3 times ULN, discontinue and do not reintroduce.
Liver symptoms check at every visit: jaundice, anorexia, nausea/GI complaints, malaise, unusual fatigue, dark urine. Any of these should trigger urgent evaluation and stopping the medication.

Suicide risk monitoring: Especially during the first 1 to 2 months and during dose increases/decreases. Watch for clinical worsening, suicidality, agitation, panic attacks, insomnia, irritability, hostility, impulsivity, akathisia, hypomania, or mania. Involve family/caregivers when appropriate.
Mood activation: Screen for bipolar disorder before treatment; monitor for hypomania/mania after starting or changing dose.
Sedation and cognitive effects: Daytime sleepiness, slowed reaction time, impaired alertness—especially when combined with other sedatives.
Orthostatic hypotension: Ask about dizziness on standing; check blood pressure sitting/standing if symptomatic or high-risk.
Function outcomes: Work/school performance, sleep quality, social functioning, and daily activity—tie continued use to measurable benefit given the liver risk.
Drug interaction review: Recheck medication lists at every visit; nefazodone’s CYP3A4 inhibition can make interactions clinically dangerous.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Nefazodone is available as oral tablets in several strengths. Dosing is typically split into two doses per day.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Nefazodone works as a serotonin modulator. In plain terms: it increases serotonin and norepinephrine signaling by inhibiting reuptake, while also blocking certain serotonin receptors (notably 5-HT2) and alpha-1 receptors. This mix can feel less “activating” for some people than classic SSRIs, but it also contributes to side effects like sedation and lightheadedness.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Nefazodone is usually not a first-line antidepressant today because of its rare but life-threatening liver failure risk and its major drug interaction profile. When it’s used, it’s often in carefully selected patients—typically after other antidepressants have failed or weren’t tolerated—and only with clear counseling about liver warning symptoms, strict interaction screening, and close follow-up early in treatment.

seo.title: Nefazodone (Serzone): Uses, Dosage, Side Effects & Liver Warning
seo.description: Nefazodone (Serzone) for depression: dosing (100 mg BID start, up to 600 mg/day), when it starts working (1-2 weeks early, 4-6 weeks full), common side effects, major drug interactions, suicidality monitoring, and the rare but serious liver failure warning.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Nefazodone is used to treat major depression. In practice, it’s usually not a first-choice antidepressant because it carries a rare but serious risk of liver failure and has major drug interactions. When it’s used, it’s typically for carefully selected patients who need an alternative option.

faqs.q: How long does nefazodone take to work?
faqs.a: Some people notice early changes within 1 to 2 weeks, but fuller antidepressant benefits usually build over 4 to 6 weeks. If nothing is improving by then, your prescriber will typically reassess the plan.

faqs.q: Why does nefazodone have a liver warning?
faqs.a: Because there have been cases of life-threatening hepatic failure in people taking nefazodone, including cases requiring liver transplant or resulting in death. The reported U.S. rate is about 1 case of liver failure leading to transplant or death per 250,000 to 300,000 patient-years of treatment. It’s rare, but severe enough that it changes how the medication is prescribed.

faqs.q: What liver symptoms should I watch for on nefazodone?
faqs.a: Call your prescriber immediately if you notice jaundice (yellow skin or eyes), loss of appetite, nausea or other GI complaints, unusual fatigue, malaise, dark urine, or abdominal discomfort. These are not “push through it” symptoms with this medication.

Like other antidepressants, it carries a boxed warning that antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thinking and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults (up to age 24) in short-term studies. People of all ages should be monitored closely for worsening depression, suicidality, or unusual behavior changes—especially in the first 1 to 2 months and during dose changes. Nefazodone is not approved for pediatric use.

faqs.q: What is a typical nefazodone dose for depression?
faqs.a: A common adult starting dose is 100 mg twice daily, although some guidance suggests starting lower (50 to 100 mg/day total) depending on tolerability. The dose may be increased gradually by 100 to 200 mg/day at intervals of at least 1 week to a usual total daily dose of 150 to 600 mg/day in two divided doses.

faqs.q: Do I need to taper nefazodone when stopping?
faqs.a: Often, yes—especially if you’ve been on it for more than a few weeks or you’re at higher doses. A gradual taper (commonly over about 2 weeks after ≥4 weeks of treatment) can reduce discontinuation symptoms and help detect relapse early. If you get significant withdrawal symptoms, your prescriber may have you return to the prior dose and taper more slowly.

faqs.q: What medications should not be combined with nefazodone?
faqs.a: Nefazodone has major interactions and is contraindicated with several specific medications listed in labeling (including carbamazepine, cisapride, terfenadine, astemizole, and pimozide). Triazolam is generally contraindicated. Always review your full medication list with your prescriber and pharmacist before starting or changing nefazodone.

faqs.q: Can nefazodone trigger mania if I have bipolar disorder?
faqs.a: Yes. Any antidepressant can precipitate mania or hypomania in vulnerable patients. People presenting with depression should be screened for bipolar disorder, and any sudden decrease in need for sleep, increased energy, impulsivity, or unusually elevated/irritable mood after starting or increasing the dose should be reported immediately.

faqs.q: Is nefazodone safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Data are limited compared with more commonly used antidepressants, so it’s generally not first-line for people who are pregnant or breastfeeding—especially if they’re treatment-naive. That said, untreated depression also carries serious risks, and decisions should be made through shared decision-making that weighs relapse risk, prior medication response, and infant factors. If breastfeeding while taking nefazodone is considered, infants should be monitored for sedation and poor feeding.
